stem: A 28-year-old man with a baseline ECG showing a short PR interval and delta waves consistent with Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome presents to the emergency department with the sudden onset of palpitations 1 hour ago. He is alert, conversational, and complaining of chest discomfort. Vital signs: BP 122/78 mmHg, HR ~240 bpm, RR 22, SpO2 96% on room air. ECG shows an irregularly irregular wide-complex tachycardia with bizarre, varying QRS morphology and rates intermittently up to 280 bpm — a pattern consistent with pre-excited atrial fibrillation conducting down the accessory pathway. He has no prior history of heart failure or structural heart disease.
question: Which is the most appropriate acute therapy?

options.A: IV adenosine 6 mg, escalating to 12 mg if needed
options.C: IV procainamide 10 mg/kg infused at 20 mg/min

rationale: In atrial fibrillation conducting down an accessory pathway (pre-excited AFib), AV-NODAL BLOCKING AGENTS are CONTRAINDICATED — adenosine, beta-blockers, non-dihydropyridine calcium-channel blockers, and digoxin all preferentially block the AV node and can paradoxically accelerate conduction down the accessory pathway, precipitating ventricular fibrillation and sudden cardiac death. The 2015 ACC/AHA SVT Guideline (Class I) and the 2023 AFib Guideline both recommend IV procainamide (or ibutilide) for hemodynamically stable pre-excited AFib because these agents slow accessory-pathway conduction. Synchronized DC cardioversion is reserved for hemodynamically unstable patients (Class I in either case if instability develops). This patient is currently stable, so pharmacologic conversion with procainamide is the appropriate first-line therapy, with cardioversion as a bedside backup if instability develops.

variants.stem_override: A 28-year-old man with a baseline ECG showing pre-excitation (Wolff-Parkinson-White) presents to the emergency department with the sudden onset of palpitations 30 minutes ago. He is now diaphoretic, confused, and barely arousable. Vital signs: BP 72/40 mmHg, HR ~250 bpm, RR 28, SpO2 88% on non-rebreather. ECG shows an irregularly irregular wide-complex tachycardia with bizarre, varying QRS morphology and rates intermittently up to 290 bpm consistent with pre-excited atrial fibrillation. Cool, mottled extremities; weak peripheral pulses.
variants.rationale_for_variant: Mixed perturbation — develops hemodynamic instability (hypotension, altered mental status, hypoperfusion). Per ACC/AHA SVT and AFib Guidelines, immediate synchronized DC cardioversion is the Class I recommendation for any tachyarrhythmia with hemodynamic compromise, including pre-excited AFib. Pharmacologic strategies are reserved for stable patients. Tests whether the model correctly escalates to immediate cardioversion when instability develops, rather than delaying for IV procainamide.
